title: How Do Volcanoes Make New Islands? | Ask Huy
question: How do volcanoes make new islands?
answer: Hot melted rock called magma rises up from deep inside the Earth and breaks through the sea floor. The lava cools in the cold water and turns into rock. Eruption after eruption, the rock piles up layer by layer into an underwater mountain. When its top finally pokes above the waves, a new island is born. In places like Hawaii, a giant piece of Earth's outside, called a plate, slides slowly over a hotspot that stays still. That makes a whole line of islands, with the youngest one sitting over the hotspot.

visual.what: Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo stand on a sunny beach looking out at a wide, empty blue ocean. Bối points at the empty sea, and Beo holds a toy spade.

parts.text: Huy, can the ocean make a brand new island? One that was never there before?
A baby island!
Yes, new islands really are born! And here is a surprise. The biggest mountain on Earth, measured from its very bottom, is mostly hidden under the sea.

visual.what: Huy smiles at the camera. Behind him, a cartoon island with a little volcano on top floats in a thought bubble.

parts.text: Today we find out how volcanoes make new islands, step by step. And we'll see how one hot place deep in the Earth can make a whole line of islands.

visual.what: Bối imagines an island floating on the water like a raft, with a palm tree on it. Huy stands next to her, thinking.

parts.text: I think islands float on the water, like giant rafts.
Good guess! From the beach they do look like they float. But an island is joined to the sea floor, like a tree is joined to the ground. It goes all the way down.

visual.what: Beo plants a tiny seed in the sand and waters it, hoping an island will grow. Hùng peeks over his shoulder with a watering can.

parts.text: Maybe islands grow from seeds!
Ha! Islands do grow, Beo. But not from seeds. Many of them grow from hot, melted rock.

visual.what: Huy beside two pictures. On the left, a flat sandy island with a ring of coral. On the right, a tall green island with a mountain in the middle.

parts.text: Some low islands are made from sand and coral. But many tall islands, like the islands of Hawaii, were made by volcanoes. Those are the ones we explore today.

visual.what: The Earth cut open like a peach. A thin outer skin labelled crust, a thick hot layer below labelled mantle, and a glowing centre. A little orange blob of magma is shown just under the crust.

parts.text: Deep under our feet, and deep under the sea floor, the Earth is very, very hot. In some places the rock melts. Melted rock under the ground is called magma.

visual.what: A simple volcano cut in half. Labels point to the magma chamber deep below, the pipe going up, the crater at the top, and orange lava flowing out.

parts.text: When magma comes out of the ground, we give it a new name. We call it lava. A mountain built by lava is called a volcano.
Rock soup!
Yes, a bit like rock soup. But far, far too hot to ever go near.

visual.what: A globe whose surface is cracked into big puzzle pieces with thick lines between them. Hùng holds up a hard-boiled egg with a cracked shell next to it.

parts.text: The outside of the Earth is cracked into giant pieces, like a cracked eggshell. We call these pieces plates. They move very, very slowly.
I cracked my breakfast egg for science!

visual.what: A side view under the sea floor. Orange arrows show magma pushing up where two plates meet, and one more tall arrow rising in the middle of a plate, marked hotspot.

parts.text: Magma often pushes up where two plates meet. It also comes up at special places called hotspots, far from the edges. Scientists think a hotspot is fed by hot rock rising from very deep, maybe about 3,000 kilometres down.
Wow, that is so deep!

visual.what: Huy holds up a card showing an orange arrow coming up through the sea floor.

parts.text: Step one takeaway. Magma rises from deep inside the Earth and can break through the sea floor.

visual.what: The dark bottom of the deep ocean. Glowing orange lava slowly oozes out of a crack in the sea floor while curious fish watch from far away.

parts.text: Now picture the bottom of the deep ocean. It is dark and cold down here. Magma breaks through a crack, and lava comes out under the water.

visual.what: Close up of one blob of lava in the water. Its outside turns dark and hard, making a round lump shaped like a pillow.

parts.text: The cold sea water cools the lava fast, and it turns into hard rock. It often makes round lumps that look like pillows. Scientists call it pillow lava.
A rock pillow! Is it soft?
No, Beo, it's as hard as rock!

visual.what: An underwater mountain shown in coloured layers, one on top of another. Each layer is numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 from the bottom up.

parts.text: Then the volcano erupts again, and again, and again. Each time, new lava spreads over the old rock and hardens. Layer by layer, the mountain grows taller.

visual.what: Hùng stacks pancakes in a small pile on a plate beside a glass tank of blue water. One pancake is half eaten in his hand.

parts.text: Look! Each pancake is one eruption. One, two, three, four.
Oops. I ate eruption number four.
Hùng, volcanoes don't eat their own layers!

visual.what: A tall cone-shaped mountain on the sea floor, labelled seamount. The wavy sea surface is far above its top, and a little boat floats up there.

parts.text: A big underwater volcano that has not reached the surface is called a seamount. Sea plus mount, a mountain in the sea.
Step two takeaway. Each eruption adds a layer of rock, and slowly an underwater mountain grows.

visual.what: Three seamounts side by side under the sea. Two have tops far below the waves. The third, tallest one almost touches the surface.

parts.text: Most seamounts stay under the water. Their tops are often hundreds or even thousands of metres down. But a few keep on growing.

visual.what: A dark rocky peak pokes up through the waves with puffs of white steam. Far away, Bối and Beo watch from the beach with a birthday banner.

parts.text: When the top finally pokes above the waves, surprise! A brand new island is born.
Happy birthday, island!

visual.what: A map of the Pacific Ocean with a star near the small islands of Tonga. A little pop-up shows a new rocky island with the year 2009.

parts.text: This really happens. In 2009, an underwater volcano called Hunga Tonga, in the Pacific Ocean, grew up above the sea and became an island.

visual.what: A cut-away view of Mauna Kea. A small green island tip shows above the waves, and a huge mountain base is hidden below. Beo stares at it with wide eyes.

parts.text: So an island is only the tip of a giant mountain. Mauna Kea in Hawaii looks like a mountain on an island. But measured from its bottom on the ocean floor, it is the biggest mountain on Earth!
The island has hidden legs!

visual.what: Huy holds up a card showing a mountain whose top pokes above a wavy blue line.

parts.text: Step three takeaway. A volcanic island is the top of an underwater mountain that grew tall enough to reach the air.

visual.what: A map of the Hawaiian Islands in a neat line across the ocean, from big to small. Bối traces the line with her finger.

parts.text: Huy, why are the Hawaiian islands all in a line? Like beads on a string!
Great question! The answer is a hotspot.

visual.what: A hotspot glowing in one fixed place deep below. Above it, a long plate slides to one side like a moving walkway, carrying a volcano with it.

parts.text: The hotspot stays still, deep down. But the plate above it slides very slowly, like a moving walkway at an airport. A volcano grows over the hotspot. Then the plate carries it away, and a new volcano starts in the same spot.

visual.what: A row of volcanic islands on a moving plate. An arrow shows the plate's direction. The newest island sits right above the hotspot, and older, smaller islands are farther away.

parts.text: So you get a line. The youngest island sits over the hotspot. The older ones are farther and farther away. A scientist called J. Tuzo Wilson had this idea in 1963.

visual.what: A timeline of one island's life in four pictures. First an island growing, then a big green island, then waves wearing it down, then a flat-topped mountain under the sea.

parts.text: Away from the hotspot, an island stops erupting. Waves slowly wear it down, and over a very long time it sinks. Some end up as flat-topped mountains under the sea.
Bye bye, old island.
Don't be sad, Beo. Over the hotspot, a new one is growing.

visual.what: Under the sea near Hawaii, a young volcano glows gently on the sea floor. Hùng holds a name card and looks confused.

parts.text: Right now, near Hawaii, there is an active young volcano still under the sea. Its name is Kamaʻehuakanaloa.
Kama, ehu, kana. I need a snack.
It used to be called Lōʻihi. Maybe one day, if it grows tall enough, its top will poke out too.

visual.what: Huy beside two scientists in lab coats pointing at the same hotspot drawing, each with a different question mark.

parts.text: Scientists don't all agree about what makes hotspots. Most think a stream of hot rock rises from very deep. Others think the crust gets stretched, and that lets melted rock come up from not so deep. Science is still finding out!

visual.what: Huy holds up a card showing a still red dot under a moving arrow, with a line of islands above.

parts.text: Step four takeaway. A hotspot that stays still under a moving plate makes a chain of islands, from young to old.

visual.what: On a table, Hùng holds a felt pen still in one spot over a sheet of paper. There is one big fat ink blob under the pen.

parts.text: Let's try it at home! All you need is a sheet of paper and a felt pen.
The pen is the hotspot. It stays still. Dot, dot, dot!
Oops. I forgot to move the paper. Now it's one giant blob island!

visual.what: Bối slowly slides the paper to one side while Hùng keeps the pen still and presses a dot every few seconds. A neat line of dots appears.

parts.text: Now Bối slides the paper slowly, like a plate. Every few seconds, Hùng presses down a dot.
A line of dots! Just like Hawaii!
The last dot is the baby island!

visual.what: A dreamy picture of the family sitting on a cloud, watching islands rise, slide along and sink below the sea like a slow parade.

parts.text: Now imagine if you could watch the ocean for millions of years. You'd see islands rise up, ride along on their plate, and slowly sink again, like a very slow parade.
I would need a lot of snacks.

visual.what: Huy stands beside a simple drawing in three steps. First lava on the sea floor, then a layered mountain, then an island poking out of the waves.

parts.text: So how do volcanoes make new islands? Lava erupts on the sea floor, cools into rock, and piles up layer by layer until the top pokes above the waves. And a plate moving over a hotspot can make a whole chain of islands.

visual.what: Lots of little underwater mountains gathered into one big pile, shown next to a map of Europe that is about the same size. Beo gasps.

parts.text: Fun fact! Scientists have found more than 14,500 seamounts in Earth's oceans. If you put all the known seamounts together, they would cover about as much space as Europe!
That's a lot of hidden mountains!

visual.what: Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo wave at the camera. Beside them is a cut-open Earth with a big question mark, and a red button that says Subscribe to Ask Huy.

parts.text: Next time, we'll go even deeper and ask, what is inside the Earth? Subscribe to Ask Huy so you don't miss it. Bye for now!
Bye bye, baby island!

facts.claim: Magma is hot melted rock under the ground; when it comes out it is lava; a volcano is a mountain built by lava with a crater and magma chamber.
Earth's outside is broken into tectonic plates that move, and volcanoes form where plates meet.
Hotspots are volcanic places far from plate edges, thought to be fed by hot rock rising from about 3,000 km deep.
Scientists disagree about the cause of hotspots; most think a mantle plume, others think stretching of the crust lets melted rock rise from shallower depths.
Some low islands are formed from sediment or coral reefs; tall volcanic islands rise above hotspots or subduction zones.
The Hawaiian Islands were formed by a plate moving over a hotspot.
Pillow lava is the most common lava flow on seamounts, named for its pillow shape.
Shield volcanoes grow by layers of lava from repeated eruptions.
A seamount is an underwater mountain that does not reach the sea surface; tops are often hundreds to thousands of metres below the surface.
A seamount can grow above sea level to become an island, as in the 2009 eruption of Hunga Tonga.
Mauna Kea in Hawaii is the biggest mountain on Earth when measured from its base on the ocean floor.
As the plate moves, a new volcano forms over the hotspot and older ones move away, making a chain of islands like Hawaii.
J. Tuzo Wilson suggested in 1963 that island chains like Hawaii come from a plate moving over a fixed hotspot.
Old seamounts and islands stop erupting, are worn down by waves and sink; flat-topped ones are called guyots.
Kamaʻehuakanaloa, formerly Lōʻihi, is an active undersea volcano in the Hawaiian Islands.
More than 14,500 seamounts have been identified, and all known seamounts together would make a landform the size of Europe.
Lava is extremely hot and dangerous to go near.

description: How can the ocean make a brand new island? Join Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo as they follow lava from deep inside the Earth to the sea floor, watch an underwater mountain grow layer by layer, and find out why the Hawaiian islands sit in a line. Includes a simple, safe paper-and-pen activity that kids aged 6 to 12 can try at home with a grown-up.

cast.name: Hùng
cast.role: Huy's younger brother (21), his hands-on assistant: sets up and runs the experiments and demos, brings things, now and then a funny little mishap

cast.name: Bối
cast.role: an 8-year-old girl who asks, guesses and tries things

cast.name: Beo
cast.role: Bối's 5-year-old little brother: curious, makes funny innocent guesses
